description: Successful completion of this class should enable students to operate their agricultural or industrial facilities in compliance with applicable environmental regulations. U.S. and European practices will be compared. Introduce students to the Clean Air Act, National Ambient air quality standards, New Source Performance standards and the permitting process. Students should gain an understanding of pollution emissions and state of the art control equipment and best operating practices.

course_title: The World has a Drinking Problem: Global Water Scarcity
description: Lecture and group learning activities result in developing informed opinions and facilitate study of how drinking water maintains and improves human health, availability of fresh water throughout the world; population changes, cultural influences, and political power affect quality, distribution, and cost of water for children, rural communities, and under-represented peoples.

Successful completion of this class should enable students to design and permit air pollution abatement systems, to include cyclones, bag filters and scrubbers, in compliance with applicable environmental regulations. U.S. and European practices will be compared. Introduce students to the Clean Air Act, National Ambient air quality standards, New Source Performance standards and the permitting process. Students should gain an understanding of pollution emissions and state of the art control equipment and best operating practices.

Introduction to Bioenvironmental Sciences (3cr) provides students with a broad survey of environmental science with an emphasis on scientific literacy, current events, global and international issues, and historic context.

This course is the gateway to solving many of the problems relating to water that civil engineers take on. These problems include flooding, droughts, water supply and distribution, fire protection, pollution control, etc. We will build on your knowledge of fluid mechanics and add some new theory on the subject that will lead us into basic design issues. We will also begin studying “hydrology,” which is probably new to many of you as a formal study, but you’ve been exposed to it all your lives.

This course is the gateway to solving many of the problems relating to water that civil engineers take on. These problems include flooding, droughts, water supply and distribution, fire protection, pollution control, etc. We will build on your knowledge of fluid mechanics and add some new theory on the subject that will lead us into basic design issues. We will also begin studying “hydrology,” which is probably new to many of you as a formal study, but you’ve been exposed to it all your lives.

Forest Ecology discusses the fundamental interactions between organisms with one another and with their environment, and the processes that tie them together into an ecosystem, using forests as an example. You will learn the significance of the feedback between organisms’ individual life history, structure, and function with their environment, succession, food webs, and biogeochemical cycling. We will discuss how the fundamental principles governing organismal growth and interactions with their environment are used in present-day forest management, resource conservation, and climate mitigation efforts.

Principles of ecology using a holistic approach treating plants, animals, and humans as one integrated whole; composition, structure, nutrient cycles and energetics of biotic communities; adaptions to environmental factors; biotic relationships; and problems of environmental quality and resource use.

Introduction to the design and development of computer applications for engineers; computation to enhance problem-solving abilities; basic concepts of software design through the implementation and debugging of student-written programs; introduction to engineering majors, career exploration, engineering practice within realistic constraints, e.g. economic, environmental, ethical, health and safety, and sustainability; pathways to success in engineering.

A field-based course conducted in Costa Rica at the Texas A&M Soltis Center for Research and Education that examines the diversity, behavior, and natural history of tropical insects. Emphasis is placed on collecting insects, specimen preparation and identification, behavioral observation, and experimental research, along with the development of skills in field note-keeping, teamwork, and scientific communication. The course provides direct experience with tropical ecosystems and addresses the challenges associated with studying and conserving biodiversity.

This is an introductory, core-curriculum course for non-entomology majors emphasizing the roles insects have played in the development of human society. This includes roles in human health, food production and storage, art, music and architecture. The historic, present day and future roles that insects will have on sustainability in underdeveloped, developing and developed societies will be discussed.

Introductory course on honey bee biology, evolution, management, and preservation. ENTO 320 uses honey bees as a model organism to learn about the scientific process, as well as basic and applied concepts in biology, entomology, sociobiology, and the evolution of communication.

This course provides an overview of the ways arthropods impact global public health and wellbeing, either directly or through the pathogens they transmit. It aims to provide a broad perspective, covering pertinent public health issues from a local to global scale. A historical perspective will be integrated throughout, and the impact of globalization, migration, poverty, and culture on pathogen transmission by arthropods and associated diseases will be discussed.

course_title: Directed Studies: Workshop in Environmental Studies
description: This study abroad aims to provide students with a professionalizing academic experience. The topic for the Summer 2025 semester study abroad experience will be to investigate issues surrounding one of the megatrends of our time: urbanization. The study abroad experience will: (1) encourage undergraduate students at TAMU to participate in international collaborative research training in Germany (Berlin) and Sweden (Gävle and Stockholm); (2) introduce undergraduate students to careers in environmental consulting, urban planning, land use planning, and other related fields; and (3) provide research training in systems and futures thinking to undergraduate students.

Exploration into the spatial variability and human geography of exposure to environmental hazards in U.S. and international contexts; emphasizes environmental equity and environmental racism as it relates to occupational, leisure, and residential geography.

Geography 205 is an introductory course in physical geography that explores environmental change and the structures of knowledge around environmental topics. The purpose of this course is to apply a systems perspective on attributes, elements, and connections within the earth’s physical environment and to learn how and why the environment changes at multiple spatial and temporal scales. A systems approach is used to structure our approach to the atmosphere, cryosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere

This course takes an earth systems approach to studying the planet we inhabit. All of the earth’s spheres—the atmosphere (weather & climate), hydrosphere (water in all its forms), lithosphere (earth’s surface), and biosphere (living organisms, plants and animals)—are examined in detail. The lectures explore the complex interactions between these spheres as well as how they affect and are affected by humans. We will cover the fundamental principles that are necessary for understanding earth systems science, also referred to as physical geography.

Overview of the ocean environment, interrelation of the sub-disciplines of ocean sciences, importance of the oceans to human beings, human impact on the oceans. Class discussion of current events of relevance to the oceans.

Public health core knowledge address factors that pose risks and hazards in homes and workplaces; methods for defining environmental contamination; identifying contaminants, pathogens and toxins; assessing risks and causality; ameliorating hazards.

This course has been designed to introduce students to land management within the private/public land interface. Developing skills to understand, and therefore manage, the interface between stakeholders will be the primary focus of this course. Students will become familiar with the issues and practices regarding natural resource management within the public/private land interface related to ranching and livestock production, wildlife-based enterprises, endangered species management, and other areas of natural resources

Study and compare human and natural ecosystems using diversity, interrelations, cycles, and energy as the conceptional organization; central themes of the course are natural resource stewardship, scientific application, and environmental sustainability. Students will apply tools of wildlife management as a framework for natural resource management, exploring how these tools reflect and impact societal order and economic considerations locally and globally.

course_title: Social and Ethical Aspects of International Cropping Systems/Ethical Aspects of International Agricultural Systems
description: Philosophical basis of ethical decisions; includes slavery, war, population growth, migration, farm workers, chemical inputs, genetically modified organisms, soil and water conservation and protection of wild species.

This course provides a comprehensive overview of several important concepts related to urban transportation planning. The topics covered in this course are organized into three themes. Theme A sets the scene for our study in urban transportation planning. Trends in public transportation, urban development, relevant legislation, and public policy decision-making processes will be studied as a general background for transportation planning. In Theme B, we discuss some of the most common aspects of transportation planning, such as travel demand analysis, transportation finance, and the interactions between land use and transportation. Theme C addresses various compelling issues challenging the current transportation planners and policymakers.

Issues pertaining to the evolution and development of cities and urban regions; examines the socioeconomic, cultural and physical development of urban areas; addresses contemporary problems such as racial tension, unemployment and poverty, housing, pollution and environmental sustainability, traffic and congestion, land use, crime, public health, and other quality of life issues.

course_title: Smart Cities: Bit, Bots, and Beyond
description: The global market for smart cities is growing exponentially. Transformative technologies (e.g., ICT, IoT, data analytics, AI, automation) can promote livability, productivity, and sustainability of cities. With supportive policy frameworks, we can turn these technologies into robust solutions for challenges of climate change, transportation, aging population, governance, economic growth, and social inclusion. However, there is a significant shortage of professionals who can serve as “bridge persons” between technology and local communities.

Determinants of land use patterns; classification of uses; idealized conceptual alternatives; location and size criteria; mapping; comprehensive planning process, relationship to circulation planning.

This course introduces students to the history of contemporary urban and regional planning, and how the evolving forms of cities and regions pose opportunities and/or challenges for planners. This course helps students to understand what a city is, how cities work, why and how cities evolve, bringing in urban spatial structure and function, their evolution over time, and forces that influence change. It covers theories of urban expansion, the history of urbanization and suburbanization in the United States, and local and global forces that shape urban structure. With an understanding of key social, economic, political, and technological forces that shape city form and function, students of this course will analyze spatial patterns and socioeconomic functions of cities and regions.
Air breathing propulsion; design and analysis of inlets, compressors, combustors, turbines and nozzles; application to aeronautical, aerospace, ground transportation and energy.

Design, installation, operation, and management of landscape irrigation systems. Includes principles of hydraulics such as friction losses and design pressure, customer service, site evaluation, and a final design project. Fulfills the education requirements for obtaining a State of Texas Irrigation License.

course_title: Designing and Delivering Effective Youth Programs
description: Design and Deliver Youth Programs. Introduction to the concepts of program design for youth programs; focuses on key programming issues; development of implementation plans; overview of equipment and facilities; focus on program flexibility, risk management and evaluation (formative and summative).

The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the history of youth development, program emphases and practices of major youth serving organizations, and core competencies necessary for all youth workers. This course is an introduction to the fundamental concepts of youth development practices, programs, organizations, and services. Through this course you will develop a critical understanding of the changing views of adolescence and youth culture in the United Sates, as well as the ways that community settings influence the youth development process. This course will provide an overview of youth development theories and principles of positive youth development. We will discuss aspects of youth development programs, including the goals, program emphases, and developmental outcomes associated with participation in youth development programs.

Selected topics on the diversity of human resources in agriculture and an emphasis on working in a multicultural society. Will seek to develop an awareness towards other cultures; explore the interrelationships between the contributions of diversity on an individual, state, national and global levels.

The course will provide students with an introduction to the fields of Social and Cultural Anthropology. We will examine the numerous dimensions by which human cultures vary, including economy and subsistence, family formation, religion, language, political structure, gender relationships, and many more. We will also explore different schools of thought that attempt to explain how and why cultures vary the way they do along these dimensions around the world.

course_title: Peoples and Cultures of the World
description: Survey of human cultures around the world using case studies of customs and cultural organization; case studies exemplifying contrasting types of cultures and societies. 3 credit hours. There are no prerequisites for this course.

This course will provide students with an introduction to anthropology. Anthropology is the social science dedicated to the holistic and relativistic investigation of human life. The course will begin with an introduction to anthropology, followed by a detailed introduction to its four subfields (Biological, Archaeology, Cultural and Linguistic).

This course focuses on the integration of research, design, technology, and graphics, to elevate their proficiency and effectiveness in these core areas. Students will explore research methodologies, architectural theories, and contemporary trends within the discipline and practice of architecture and design. An essential objective is to refine their skills in these key areas of the design process and create a framework for informed design decisions. Design challenges provide opportunity to apply acquired knowledge and fostering critical thinking. The course integrates advanced tools and software, while emphasizing graphics techniques for compelling visual communication. Advanced graphics techniques are emphasized for effective visual communication. The synthesis of these elements ensures that students exit with an enriched skill set, poised to navigate the complexities of professional architectural practice.

Architectural design principles; development of skills in perception, thought and craft as they apply to the formation of two- and three-dimensional relationships. At the end of the semester, students are expected to have a visual vocabulary of drawing and abstract architectonic representation methods and the way they relate to the design process and its presentation. This course will cover methodologies and workflows for both analog and digital skills used to represent (visually express) and communicate design.

This course is designed to academically support students co-enrolled in ENGL 104 with any additional skills needed for compliance with the Texas Success Initiative. Instruction is based on the student’s skill level and progression with graded assignments. The ultimate goal in this course is to provide the students with resources that are needed for succeeding in college-level academics, specifically in ENGL 104.

course_title: Special Topics: Academic Component of Hullabaloo U for Gateway
description: ASCC 289 is a study of effective learning strategies and an introduction to campus resources designed for students participating in the Gateway program.

Structure, energy and motions of the atmosphere; climate; fronts and cyclones; atmospheric stability; clouds and precipitation; severe storms. Basic physical and atmospheric principles will need to be addressed first to provide context for understanding weather and climate, including the fun parts of severe and hazardous weather.

Exploration of applications of data analytics, machine learning, and deep learning in health sciences and biomedical data; topics include theoretical foundations, algorithms and methods of deriving valuable insights from data, predictive health analysis, electronic health records, medical image analysis.

Examination of microscopy and clinical imaging modalities in biomedical applications across intracellular to whole body length scales; microscopy topics include optical, electron, scanning probe, infrared, intravital, and other techniques; clinical imaging techniques to be covered include x-ray, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, computed and positron emission tomography, and other specialized clinical imaging.

Operating systems and distributed systems fields that form the basis of cloud computing, such as virtualization, key-value storage solutions, group membership, failure detection, peer-to-peer systems, datacenter networking, resource management, and scalability; popular frameworks such as MapReduce and HDFS, and case studies on failure determination.

Hardware/software evolution leading to contemporary operating systems; basic operating systems concepts; methods of operating systems design and construction including algorithms for CPU scheduling, memory and general resource allocation, process coordination and management; case studies of several operating systems

Basic terminology, concepts, technology, and trends of cybersecurity; foundations of cybersecurity to include cryptography, public key infrastructure, standards and protocols, physical security, network fundamentals; workings of systems, networks, infrastructure; legal and ethical issues in cybersecurity.

Extend prior programming knowledge to create computer programs that solve problems; use the C++ language; apply computational thinking to enhance problem-solving; analyze, design, and implement computer programs; use basic and aggregate data types to develop functional and object-oriented solutions; develop classes that use dynamic memory and avoid memory leaks; learn error handling strategies to develop more secure and robust programs.

Computer architects have been striving to improve performance and efficiency since the first stored program computer was designed half a century ago. Superscalar execution is a key technique towards this aim. Superscalar processors issue more than one instruction per cycle. Most modern microprocessors from the latest smartphone ARM processors, to Intel Skylake I7s, to IBM’s latest Power8 employ superscalar issue and other instruction-level parallelism techniques to enhance their performance. This course examines the tradeoffs and design considerations in the design of superscalar or instruction level parallel (ILP) microprocessors. The course will also explore other current microarchitectural approaches to improve performance and efficiency.

This course provides an engineering application-focused introduction to Machine Learning. This course covers key machine learning concepts, guidance on selecting machine learning models, and application of python-based tools for data preparation, model development, and performance evaluation; Labs will provide practical engineering use-cases for machine learning from electronics, energy, motors, robotics, security, computer systems, and health. A final machine learning laboratory project including dataset management, ML model development, visualization, and deployment to an IoT platform will be used to showcase ML expertise.

department_full: Educational Administration and Human Resource Development
description: This course covers instructional design principles; development of instruction; contemporary issues and trends; foundations in learning research; requirements for instruction, task and needs analysis; learning situations and instructional models; hardware and software innovations; assessing instructional outcomes; factors affecting utilization.

department_full: Educational Administration and Human Resource Development
description: This course examines an overview course designed for all individuals planning to carry out HRD interventions or manage people – whether as part of human resource management (HRM), human resource development (HRD) or as a manager in another organizational function. EHRD 315 is an introduction to the systematic management of organizational assets, specifically, its human resources and the implications for designing and delivering HRD interventions.

Fundamental design processes, issues and theories relevant to design resolution and the creation of new ideas; creative thought processes from the formation of ideas through incubation to final product and future impact on the physical environment and society.

Examination of texts written in English that de-center the nation-state as the central way to organize cultural comparison; includes colonialism, economics, empire, globalization, and multiple subsections of the transnational experience. This course reads contemporary literature (fiction and poetry) to consider how various authors imagine what it means to be a global citizen, rather than just a national one. By conceptualizing what transnational literature is and how it shapes or reshapes the literary imagination, we’ll consider how contemporary writers and thinkers offer us new–and old–ways of thinking about ourselves as part of the globe.
A study of the technical aspects of embedded computer software systems, with emphasis on embedded real-time systems, programming techniques and development methodologies.

The course is designed to help students become prepared for a financially challenging world and to introduce the concepts and methods of personal financial literacy. Topics include financial well-being, financial planning, compound interest and the time value of money, inflation, taxes, banking, cultural influences on money, consumerism, credit, car and home acquistition, insurances, estate planning, investments, and retirement planning.

Field geography is a unique course that compliments the geography curriculum by engaging students in real world situations. Students have an opportunity to apply their knowledge of previously learned concepts and ideas, and students are introduced to the equipment, terminology, and techniques of working in the field. The successful outcome of this course, which is my goal, is to (1) increase your understanding of the field as geographers use the term, (2) introduce students to the procedures and equipment that are used to record and utilize field data, (3) facilitate your interest and knowledge of direct observation to appreciate the cultural and ecological diversity of our local environments.

This course will explore the science behind disasters; how they occur, the choices society makes that create or affect disasters, how certain populations are privileged during disasters by the decisions society has made, and how science informs preparation for and response to future disasters.

This course emphasizes curriculum offerings in the department of Global Languages and Cultures, a humanities approach to global studies and globalization, theories and approaches in the field of global studies to foster critical thinking. Students learn to evaluate global issues with a focus on human culture, and to connect the local to the global.

This course will focus on three primary goals: enhancing knowledge, increasing comfort, and facilitating communication about sex. You will be tasked with learning about human sexuality topics, then be able to teach human sexuality to others.

Women’s Health is designed to provide you, the student, with the opportunity to explore the health issues and health care concerns of women by identifying a broad range of health topics that are either unique to women or of special importance to women. The multidimensional roles of women as individuals, partners, mothers, nurturers, caretakers, and career persons create a need for their health status to be of vital importance. While women and men both experience similar diseases, disorders, and causes of death, women often experience these in different forms and at different stages and ages in life.

course_title: Intro to Health Disparity and Diversity
description: Intro to Health Disparity and Diversity (HLTH 236) course will explore in-depth the racial, ethnic, and cultural dimensions that underlie health and health disparities. Special attention will be paid to culture, social economic status, and governmental policies as they influence the adaptation of health practices. The aim of this course is to introduce students to important health issues that face individuals of differentracial and ethnic backgrounds. This course will address and explore a range of issuesrelated to the health status of various racial and ethnic groups.

HLTH 231, Healthy Lifestyles, introduces a variety of health issues that affect college students, including mental health, stress management, injury prevention, conflict resolution, alcohol/drug use and abuse, physical activity, nutrition, spirituality, and environmental health. Students will explore how these concepts interconnect and develop a holistic understanding of what it means to live healthfully.

course_title: Global Communities & Diverse Populations in Hospitality, Hotel Management and Tourism
description: This course will examine the impact of various demographic factors on leisure/tourism patterns of people in the United States, and the implications for hospitality, hotel management, and tourism. Students will investigate the impacts of marginalization on various groups and discuss ways to make space welcoming for all. Students will be offered the opportunity to articulate this knowledge intellectually and apply it to everyday living and practices.

Tourism principles applied at local, regional and international levels; examination of the scale, scope and organization of the industry including marketing destinations and experiences; issues related to the economic, technological and political aspects of tourism.

Management theory, best practices and functions associated within hospitality, hotel and tourism agencies; concepts and issues related to budgeting, financing, planning, organizing, leading, coordinating, controlling and staffing for profit, nonprofit and public organizations.

course_title: Foundations of Hospitality, Hotel Management and Tourism
description: Theoretical foundations of the hospitality, hotel management, and tourism profession; professional philosophy, present status, prospects for the future and the role of hospitality, hotel management, and tourism in modern society.

Identification, propagation, soil management, fertilization, growth control, and protection of common garden plants: indoor ornamentals, landscape ornamentals, fruits, and vegetables; special topics include home landscaping, container gardens, bonsai, herbs and medicinal plants, and hobby greenhouse management; overview of the effects of organic and non-organic practices on the garden ecosystem.

course_title: Introduction to the Science of Health and Fitness: Pilates
description: Overview of the human body systems; interdisciplinary focus on wellness, fitness, nutrition, disease, drug use; integrated physical activity centering on principles and applications of conditioning; collect data, evaluate information, formulate plans based on findings; experience with pedometers, heart rate monitors, bioelectrical impedance devices, software and other technology; also taught at Galveston campus.

course_title: The Science of Basic Health and Fitness
description: A general overview of the human body. The scientific method is used to introduce students to the fundamentals of stress, exercise, nutrition, disease, and drug use. Interdisciplinary focus on wellness and longevity. Integrated physical activity experiences centering on principles and applications of the scientific basis of conditioning.

course_title: Legal and Social Environment of Business
description: Role of government in business and society; analysis of social policy and legal institutions; ethical problems in management decisions; administrative law; antitrust law; employment and discrimination law; regulation of business transactions; protection of property rights; regulation of information in markets including securities and product safety; international business law.

course_title: Care of the Older Adult for the RN
description: The student will develop competencies and knowledge necessary for providing care and promote health aging in the older adult.

course_title: Health Promotion Across the Lifespan for the RN
description: This course emphasizes the role of the nurse in health promotion across multiple settings with diverse populations. The student will apply principles of teaching/learning, case management, and genetics/genomics to improve the health of general and vulnerable populations.

course_title: Pathophysiology and Pharmacology for the RN
description: Students will demonstrate the ability to incorporate the principles of pathophysiology and pharmacology in planning healthcare for individuals across the lifespan.

course_title: Application of Evidence Based Practice for the RN
description: This course is a study of basic research methodologies and an in depth examination of the professional nurse’s role in the application of evidence into clinical practice

course_title: Nursing Dimensions and Informatics for the RN
description: This course is designed to build on the informatics knowledge and skills of the practicing nurse. Emphasis is placed on the application of the ANA Standards for Nursing Informatics and Professional Practice and incorporation of information technology to support patient care and clinical decision-making. The course will assist the students to develop the professional role by incorporation of the philosophy of nursing, nursing theory, and clinical reasoning. The nurse’s role in interprofessional practice will be explored. The influence of ethics and cultural/society issues on the nursing profession are explored as well as opportunities for personal and professional development.

Course reflects content that will prepare senior students for transition of entry into practice. Theories and principles concerning human behavior in organizations, with emphasis on leadership roles encountered in professional nursing practice. Senior nursing students in collaboration with nursing faculty refine coordination of care for a diverse population of clients. A clinical practicum will focus on synthesizing and refining skills in the delivery and management of nursing care to various groups of clients. Concepts of clinical decisionmaking, and inter-professional dynamics are incorporated in the context of legal, ethical, and evidence-based practice.

The nursing process is utilized in the study of community/public health nursing practice and common health problems encountered in community settings. Health promotion, maintenance, counseling and coordination of care are utilized in providing care to individuals, families, aggregates and populations in community settings. Principles and skills of public health nursing practice are used to assess a community’s health and diagnose community health needs.

course_title: Nursing Care of Children and Families
description: A study of the factors influencing health promotion, protection and maintenance of infants, children and adolescents; examination of family theory, growth and development, primary health care, and acute, chronic, and terminal conditions; clinical experience in caring for healthy, atrisk, acutely and chronically ill infants, children, adolescents and their families.

Demonstrates the relevance of psychosocial nursing concepts to all areas of professional practice. Provides a conceptual integration of the nursing process, theories and research from psychosocial sciences and humanities as these relate to the care of persons with mental disorders. Clinical experience provides an opportunity for application of psychosocial concepts and methods in using the nursing process to promote optimal levels of wellness for individuals, families and target groups.

This course introduces the student to the use of the nursing process in the care of adults with chronic or non-complex illness. The course uses a systems approach to discuss the effects of illness on individual and family, and to examine the disruption of growth and development patterns across the lifespan from young adult to senior years, emphasizing the nursing process to assist adults in reaching their optimal level of wellness. The course includes clinical laboratory to allow the student the opportunity to apply theoretical concepts to clinical practice in diverse adult populations.

This course presents an overview of age-related changes including physical, emotional, social and environmental transitions in the aging family. Emphasis is placed on developmental patterns and health promotion in the population.

Principles of assessing nutrition problems in populations and planning nutrition programs to promote health in communities including nutrition education and food and nutrition policy; introduction to food and nutrition assistance programs.

This introductory course focuses on principles of nutrition with application to the physiologic needs of individuals; food sources of nutrients and selection of an adequate diet; formulation of Dietary Reference Intakes; and nutritional surveillance.

This course covers principles of accident investigation and how accidents happen in the workplace. This course integrates procedural, systematic, corrective, and formative applications for the occupational health professional.

Exploration of social determinants of population health and the socio-cultural roots of health improvement; socioeconomic, behavioral and other factors that impact human health and contribute to health improvement and health disparities.

This course discusses the history, philosophy, and development of public health. Topics include definitions of population health and wellness, determinants of health, health status indicators and measurement, community health, the core functions and essential services, and the theory and practice of health improvement. In addition, public health interventions are explored and explained, with an emphasis on public health practice.

The course material is divided into three sections. First, we will consider the different means by which governments have structured ethnic relations and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses associated with each approach. Second, we will discuss theories seeking to explain why these domestic arrangements for containing conflict have sometimes broken down and ethnic violence has emerged. Third, we will evaluate the costs and benefits of different strategies for facilitating the peaceful resolution of existing conflicts.

This course offers a comprehensive survey of major transformations in American and Western societies, exploring the forces that drive social change and the tensions that arise as a result. Through historical and contemporary perspectives, students will analyze how political, economic, environmental, and cultural dynamics have shaped global development and inequality. The course emphasizes global interdependence and the evolution of social institutions in response to shifting power structures and ideologies. Students will explore dynamics of development and globalization, with a focus on how these processes shape social, political, and environmental realities across the globe.

In this course, we will focus on how sociologists define and use the concepts of “race” and “ethnicity,” and how sociologists use theories and data to learn about race and ethnicity. This course will introduce you to the sociology of race and ethnicity, providing you with the resources needed to investigate the issues more fully. This course is not designed to teach you what to think about racial and ethnic issues, but instead how to think critically about them. This course requires you to use your critical thinking, reading, and writing skills in the analysis of materials regarding racial and ethnic minority groups in the United States.

This course examines an encompassing perspective of diversity and inclusion within North American and international sport organizations. Specifically, the course provides students with an analysis and understanding of the various ways that people within sport organizations can differ, and how power differences based on this diversity impact life and work experiences, opportunities, and outcomes. The course treats issues of the non-dominant, historically underrepresented elements of U.S. society, with a particular emphasis placed on racial, ethnic, religion, sexual orientation, and gender issues.

course_title: Introduction to GIS in Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning
description: This is an introductory course in Geographic Information Systems (GIS). In it, students will develop a clear understanding of fundamental concepts, principles, and functions of GIS. Topics of emphasis include cartography, coordinate systems, data acquisition, data accuracy, database development, and spatial analysis. Through regularly scheduled readings and exercises, students will build proficiency in the use of GIS software and related hardware.

Study abroad course that focuses on healthy lifestyles and life expectancy around the world; explores cultural competency, as contextualized by the Association of American Medical Colleges, within a global context; and emphasizes how societal infrastructure, along with cultural values, can impact individual health and the experience of aging.

course_title: Special Topics: Communication Skills in Healthcare
description: This course will offer an introduction in the foundation of therapeutic behavior and communication in healthcare in the context of gathering information, working with different groups of patients and their families, conducting interviews, communicating in crisis situations, and bringing up “the bad news”. The internship includes discussion of cases, participating in interviews, participation in communication with difficult patients and discussion, simulations of challenging communicative situations.

course_title: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies
description: Historical and cross-cultural perspectives on women's roles in culture, the workplace, the family and other socio-political institutions; the social construction of gender; sexuality and racism; social control mechanisms and ideologies.

This course provides a comprehensive overview of several important concepts related to urban transportation planning. The topics covered in this course are organized into three themes. Theme A sets the scene for our study in urban transportation planning. Trends in public transportation, urban development, relevant legislation, and public policy decision-making processes will be studied as a general background for transportation planning. In Theme B, we discuss some of the most common aspects of transportation planning, such as travel demand analysis, transportation finance, and the interactions between land use and transportation. Theme C addresses various compelling issues challenging the current transportation planners and policymakers.

Study and compare human and natural ecosystems using diversity, interrelations, cycles, and energy as the conceptional organization; central themes of the course are natural resource stewardship, scientific application, and environmental sustainability. Students will apply tools of wildlife management as a framework for natural resource management, exploring how these tools reflect and impact societal order and economic considerations locally and globally.

course_title: Social and Ethical Aspects of International Cropping Systems/Ethical Aspects of International Agricultural Systems
description: Philosophical basis of ethical decisions; includes slavery, war, population growth, migration, farm workers, chemical inputs, genetically modified organisms, soil and water conservation and protection of wild species.

Theory and practice of architecture; methods and techniques used in the analysis and synthesis of concepts unique to spatial enclosure; developing responses to building systems; objects in a current cultural, physical, or social context; complex building programs, site development and design solutions integrating formally expressive visual ideas and functional planning.

Survey of the approaches, methods, and techniques applicable to English as a Second Language (ESL) instruction; examination of various facets of the language classroom; examination of ESL instruction in various socio-political contexts.

The course covers the philosophical, psychological, and sociological concepts fundamental to counseling in schools. The purpose of this course is to develop an understanding of the various roles of the professional school counselor and the various professional issues related to school counseling.
The course is designed to provide students an overview of various counseling theories and its application in a school setting.

Basic terminology, concepts, technology, and trends of cybersecurity; foundations of cybersecurity to include cryptography, public key infrastructure, standards and protocols, physical security, network fundamentals; workings of systems, networks, infrastructure; legal and ethical issues in cybersecurity.

This course introduces students to fundamental concepts in distributed systems and cloud computing, as well as covers several contemporary topics in applying cloud computing technologies. The materials of this course are based on many influential papers published at top system conferences including ACM SOCC, ACM SOSP, USENIX OSDI, USENIX ATC, USENIX Security, USENIX HotCloud, IEEE IC2E, IEEE S&P, IEEE Transactions on Cloud Computing, etc.

The course covers fundamental techniques and best pracces in deep learning, including the mathemacal building blocks of neural networks, programming languages for deep learning, deep learning for classicaon and regression, fundamental machine learning techniques for deep learning, universal workow of deep learning, deep learning for computer vision, deep learning for me-series and text, generave deep learning, hyper-parameter opmizaon, and deep reinforcement learning.

course_title: 21st Century Integration of Theory in Educational Settings
description: Examination of various curricular issues and pedagogical implications encountered by schools and educators in the 21st century classroom; examination of various theoretical frameworks needed to address those issues and implications and advance student understanding.

course_title: Developing Student’s Disciplinary Language and Reading in STEM Teaching and Learning
description: The course focuses on STEM disciplinary language and reading through an examination, analysis, and application of instructional design in secondary education. An array of topics will be covered that include: vocabulary, fluency, factors influencing comprehension, language structures, and writing to integrate, evaluate, and assimilate the learning outcomes.

course_title: Society and Education in World Perspective
description: This course is designed to examine sociocultural, economic, and political forces that impact educational systems around the world. The class will assess how different countries define and promote both teacher quality as well as teaching quality. In addition, we will examine and analyze issues, problems and solutions as they relate to providing all children with an equitable and equal education around the world. Important global issues as they relate to education and perspective consciousness will also be examined.

course_title: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) Teaching and Learning
description: Examination of integrated and multidisciplinary practice-based pedagogies; building of interdisciplinary bridges among content areas; melding sociocultural and cognitive factors influencing STEM education across K-12 levels; discussion of underrepresented groups binding best practices; development and evaluation of STEM project-based learning.

A study of the social, cultural, and historical foundations of education, this course examines how factors such as race, class, gender, language, and ability shape educational systems and influence student experiences. Designed for educators and educational leaders, the course emphasizes culturally relevant and socially just practices.

department_full: Educational Administration and Human Resource Dev.
description: The intent of this course is to develop a theoretical understanding of qualitative research and how this theory applies to your understanding of how to conduct qualitative research. This class teaches students how to collect and analyze data, conduct cross cultural research, consider ethical dimensions in conducting qualitative to evaluate sound methodological practices and design qualitative research studies.

course_title: Understanding Research from a Consumer’s Perspective
description: Introduction to skills, knowledge, and strategies for reading and interpreting research articles and reports; how to evaluate the quality of such reports; becoming competent, critical readers and consumers of research in the Social Sciences.

This course provides opportunities for learning and training experiences in the field of Public Health which are appropriate to the student’s career goals; professional supervision required. Payment for the training/field experience is optional. The following are typical examples of jobs or internships for which credit may be granted: Shadowing a public health professional (this should involve some contact with clients in practice setting); Working as a public health professional (employment as a program assistant); Working in public health research (employment in a research laboratory); public health internships.

Field placement experience where the student works closely with his/her department HBEH Applied Practice Experience coordinator and appropriate field professional(s) applying skills and techniques acquired through course work.

This course is designed to familiarize students with International Political Economy (IPE). IPE considers the flows of production, distribution, and consumption across national borders, recognizing that not just national governments play a role, but individual actors and international institutions must also be taken into account.

Techniques, principles, and theory involved in designing and implementing interactive information technologies for business based on humans’ physical, cognitive, and emotional resources; focus on application of qualitative and quantitative evaluation techniques for employee productivity with computing devices; understanding interaction phenomena at the individual, group, organizational, and global levels; accessibility, cultural, and ethical implications of human-computer enterprise-level use and impact.

Provides an understanding of the process by which a data warehouse system is designed and developed along with the underlying concepts and software systems; includes OLAP models and their differences with standard OLTP models.

Methodologies, techniques, and tools for information systems analysis and design; the analysis and logical design of business processes and management information systems focusing on the systems development life cycle; techniques for logical system design.

course_title: Introduction to Engineering Innovation in Medicine
description: An overview of concepts and topics at the intersection of engineering, medicine, and design for innovation including the design of medical technologies, rapid prototyping tools and techniques; discussion of intellectual property protection, and commercialization strategies, engineering design processes, design in a regulated environment (FDA), ideation and concept development methods, prototype development technologies, pre-clinical testing, path-to-market strategies, and entrepreneurship; includes weekly expert panel sessions, skills development workshops, and field trips.

Today’s health managers and leaders must go beyond simply accessing data; they need to turn it into actionable information that drives improvements in operations, strategy, and policy. In PHPM 603, you will build the skills necessary to analyze, interpret, display, and communicate data to support evidence‐based decision making. A special focus is placed on data visualization, essential for making sense of complexity, revealing patterns and outliers, and engaging stakeholders with clear, compelling stories.

course_title: Using Advanced Literacy to Teach and Learn Across Disciplines
description: Students enrolled in RDNG 603 consider the following: Examination of pedagogies that use literacy to help students learn across disciplines and content areas. Exploration of literacy practices including reading, writing, discussion, interpretive and critical activities for the comprehension and evaluation of new content. Strategies for teaching new literacies skills associated with information and communication technology, media, and visual reading. Examination of theoretically-grounded and empirically supported instructional methods

course_title: Designing and Developing Interventions in Special Education and Related Fields
description: This course examines the design processes used to develop instructional interventions for students with exceptionalities (e.g., disabilities, at-risk for disabilities). The course will examine (a) the use of theory as a foundation for developing interventions/logic model, (b) randomized controlled trials and multilevel experimental designs, (c) statistical analyses of results from experiments, (d) power analysis and sample size planning, (e) non-compliance, attrition, and (f) considerations for testing interventions, including budget planning. These topics will be linked to the U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences framework for developing and testing interventions.

course_title: Child Therapy: Advanced Theory and Techniques
description: Supervised experiences in public and mental health settings in the application of psychotherapy techniques with children, adolescents and families; interviewing techniques; process of therapy; advanced theoretical foundations; case management.

course_title: Instructional Strategies for Middle and High School
description: Relation of information processing models to theory and practice of planning, delivering and evaluating instruction in public school settings. Subject matter and generic competencies required for teacher certification in Texas.

A professional internship experience in biomedical sciences-related settings provides students with the opportunity for engaged learning through professional involvement and professional supervision. For course credit, a student will select an internship site and have the projected internship site and experience approved by the instructor. Typical internship sites and experiences for which credit may be granted include: Shadowing of a health professional in a clinical setting; work as a health professional; employment in a biomedical research position; volunteer in a setting related to health profession or biomedical science.
Assessment and analysis of environmental and health risk, analytical procedures, interpretation of risk factors, reporting science crisis events.
